idiom_name: BullMQ workers on one Redis-backed queue
implementation_notes: Node has no shared blocking queue, so the pattern is a library decision: each BullMQ Worker pulls jobs from the same named queue with its own concurrency setting, and starting several workers (in one process, or as separate processes/pods) puts them in competition; the library acks on promise resolution, retries failures and moves exhausted jobs aside. Multiple workers in one event loop only overlap I/O - for CPU-bound jobs the competition must span worker_threads/processes, where the queue library remains the shared channel.
pitfalls: BullMQ acks when the processor promise resolves and redelivers stalled jobs only after lock expiry, so a crashed process can duplicate work - handlers must be idempotent.
Catching errors inside the processor and returning normally acks failed jobs; throw (or job.moveToFailed) so retries and dead-lettering actually happen.
concurrency in one event loop does not add CPU parallelism: a blocking JSON/parse loop serialises all workers in that process.

variants.name: Kafka consumer group member (broker-level competition)
variants.implementation_notes: A kafkajs consumer that joins a group competes for partitions: Kafka assigns each partition - a point-to-point channel in EIP terms - to exactly one member, so throughput scales with members up to the partition count and rebalances redistribute partitions when members join or die. The client loop is still receive -> process -> commit, but ordering holds only within a partition, and the group protocol makes membership/offset management the interesting part instead of the queue.
pitfalls: More consumers than partitions leaves members idle; adding consumers past that point does not raise throughput.
Auto-commit before processing completes loses messages on crash; commit offsets only after the side effect succeeds.
Rebalances pause or revoke partitions mid-batch, so handlers must be ready to see the same message again after a rebalance.
